job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Bilal Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Bilal, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior firmware engineer at a company in Valdora that makes soil sensors for farms. I studied computer engineering, and my final project was a low-power weather node that ran for 11 months on one battery. Each day I write C code for the sensors, test it on a bench, and use an AI assistant for boilerplate and to explain datasheets. I share a house with two housemates, a barista and a teacher. Valdora is small, so there are very few other jobs like mine, and I'm on a temporary contract that ends next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's roughly what I expected, to be honest. At work I'd say AI helps with boilerplate but the real engineering still needs us at the bench. To my housemates I'd say that nothing major changes and they can stop sending me scary articles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for the long run but my short run is shaky. My contract ends next summer, my loan is about 31,000, and Valdora has one other firm that does anything like this. A plateau doesn't fix that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the assistant to move faster, and I'd use the time I save to learn power electronics and radio design. I'd also publish my weather node design as open hardware, to build a name. And I'd start saving 70 a month, even if it means I cook more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relaxed about AI, a bit tense about the contract. It's two different feelings in one chest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if your contract isn't renewed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the contract isn't renewed, I'd contact the three firms I met at the trade show, two in other cities. I'd do remote work if I could. I've already got a freelance profile with two small jobs finished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the farmer who asked for the nodes.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The weather node could become a product. A farmer in the next valley already asked if I'd build five nodes for the farm. That's not a business yet, but it's more than a hobby.

Save **70** a month by cooking more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's exciting and slightly worrying, and that the interesting question is who gets to use it. At work I'd suggest we use AI for code review and test generation, which would let a small team do more. Online I'd say that people who learn the tools will be fine and people who don't will be left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my kind of job survives longer than pure software, since firmware touches hardware and a sensor still has to work in mud. But the junior half of my job, writing standard code, goes to AI, which means less hiring for people like me. The company might keep one junior and two seniors instead of two juniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become the person at the company who sets up AI-assisted testing for the sensors. I'd also take on the field-testing side, driving to farms and fixing real devices. And I'd build my sensor node into a small kit, selling a few a month, to have a second income if my contract goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Energised, mostly. It's like a new tool arriving at the bench: I want to see what it can do before I decide what I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you are you worrying about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do worry about the people who aren't like me. My housemate Kenji teaches, and his school is already using AI for marking, with parents asking if his job is safe. I don't know what to tell him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you tell your housemate Kenji?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I told him to learn how it works so he can explain it to the kids. It isn't a full answer. But I think understanding it is the one thing that helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's huge and happening faster than anyone can prepare for. At work I'd say let's get the company's data and designs in order and use AI tools as heavily as we can, because the firms that do will survive. Online I'd say we need support for people who don't see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm anxious here, even though I like the tools. Full AGI in two years means the code I write is not my edge for much longer. Robots arrive three years after that, which is when my hardware advantage fades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save aggressively, maybe 60 percent of my pay, and I'd move my work toward things that need trust and presence: installing sensors on farms, repair, calibration. I'd accelerate the sensor kit and try to turn it into a small company with the farmer. And I'd keep my freelance profile active, so work comes from several places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A rush, mixed with a knot in my stomach. It's like standing at a start line with no idea how long the race is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you see the opportunity, if there is one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thing is that the farmers are the ones who'd benefit if the sensors were cheap and reliable. I think there's a real business in agricultural monitoring for small farms that can't afford a data team. That's the idea I'd bet on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your fallback if it doesn't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it didn't work, I'd have my parents' place, three hours away. They're not rich, but there's a room. It's a fallback, not a plan.

At work I'd push to use AI tools as **heavily** as we can, since firms that do will survive.
think: I'm **anxious** even though I like the tools, because code isn't my edge for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to build something real if you start now. At work I'd say we should use the time to train and move to products that need physical presence. Online I'd say that the next few years are a chance for small firms to move quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel it's the best of the three so far. By 2031 I'd be 27, with five years of experience using AI tools at a depth most people won't have. That should help, but I wouldn't count on it forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work on the sensor kit to get it to about 50 customers, and aim to leave my contract job in 2028 if it pays. Alongside, I'd take a part-time master's course in embedded AI, because edge devices are where the field is going. I'd also save 150 a month to cover the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Optimistic, with edges. Like planning a hike when you've seen the forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the part that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What worries me is what happens to people who are less lucky or less keen. I've got a good friend, Marek, who's a bank clerk with a baby on the way. He'd be at the sharp end, and I'm not sure what I could do except help with his CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you help your friend Marek?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to teach him the basics of using these tools. I'd also say that he should talk to his union rep, if there is one, soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years feels like a gift. I'd say that people should treat it as an invitation to learn something new every year. I'd say that at work, to friends and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In ten years I'd be 32 and could be running a small hardware company. I think that, with that much time, I'd be calm about my own work, though I'd keep an eye on the news. The decade also gives me time to pay off the loan and have a stable base.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's and work my way up to a lead role. I'd grow the sensor company slowly, with a first employee in four years. And I'd save for a deposit on a small place in the valley, near the farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and curious. I can actually see myself doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What might make you too confident?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The only thing that would bother me is if I'm too confident. People who are good with the tools tend to think everyone else is too. I need to keep listening to people who aren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably volunteer at a local coding club, helping older people use these tools. Because that's where the gap is, and I'd like to be a small part of closing it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'm adaptable, but I'm on a temporary contract in a small town with a loan, and two years doesn't leave enough time to build the business. What would help is retraining support, funding for small hardware firms and a clear date from governments.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I think we should talk more about people who aren't curious. Plenty of good people just don't have the time or the interest, and they shouldn't pay for that.

His mood moves from **anxious** at two years to calm at ten.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because it leaves too little time to grow his business before the contract ends.
